I recommend ARCH Linux, compile it yourself. But these concepts will apply to any server: (Keeping it terse, just nutshells)

Purpose:

  • Mitigate the possibility of a Ransomware attack.
  • Mitigate risk of data exposure by having a one-way path to expire data on all your public facing servers when it is no longer necessary for regular operations.

Scope:

  • Any organization which has at least one public facing server or a number of servers which have at least layer 3 connectivity to the Internet.

Overview:

The server shall be connected behind a hardware firewall outside of your own DMZ. It should be configured to accept NO incoming connections, except during pre-scheduled time intervals, and only then from only specific, private IP addresses. On Debian this would look something like using iptables, firewalld or some other firewall which has builtin time features, or simply use cron or atd to enable/disable certain firewall rules according to schedule.

The server reaches out and uses rsync or scp or whatever your backup method is preffered. You can use a DMZ based backup server to collect all the backups from various public facing systems, but it is only stored temporarily. When the "Offline" backup server pulls the data from the DMZ "Primary" backup server, it is then scrubbed or simply deleted off the Primary.

The "Offline" server stores some data in a write-once optical device, and other data on typical removable or external hard disks or NAS devices which are physically locked in a separate facility on a scheduled basis.

The Tips:

  • Several high capacity write-once media devices such as DVD Writers.
  • High quality DVD's with write-once/non-destructive characteristics. [EG no Rewriteables]
  • Scheduled maintenance windows open up connections to administrators only certain times of day/certain times of week

Following this very simple, high level design, you can ensure that your data doesn't fall prey to a 'Ransomware' attacker that got into your backup server.

I did something similar on a pair of OSX servers but with an additional two steps.

On the main fileserver add a tripwire file in the root of each shared folder such as "Do_Not_Edit.doc" with a known MD5. Assuming a ransomware attack will spider through folders the root files should be first modified. The LauchDaemon fires a simple script every 5 seconds or so that checks the MD5 of the tripwire files. A change in MD5 would indicate an attack or inadvertent edit. On detection of a change in MD5 the server is set to immediately shut down SMB file sharing to prevent further encryption of the file system so at most a virus will get 5 seconds playtime to mess with the data. User file access issues will be ignored in the attempt to preserve mission critical fileshare data. Sorry guys.
